mcqs.question: Why is it guaranteed correct to pop the smallest element across all K heap-seeded sources as the next merged output element?
options: Because the heap is rebuilt from scratch after every pop
Because K is always small enough that brute force would also work
Because every source is individually sorted, so nothing still hidden inside any source can be smaller than that source's currently exposed front element
Because all K sources are guaranteed to have the same length
mcqs.explanation: Since each source is sorted, its front element is its smallest remaining value — so the true global minimum across everything unmerged must be the smallest of all the currently-exposed fronts, which is exactly the heap's minimum. The heap is updated incrementally, not rebuilt each time, this reasoning holds regardless of K's size, and the sources don't need equal lengths for the argument to work.

mcqs.question: A k-way merge implementation pops the smallest element correctly but never pushes a replacement from the same source. What happens?
options: The merge produces a correct but slightly slower result
The heap automatically detects the missing push and fixes itself
This only causes a problem if two sources have identical values
That source silently stops contributing after its first element, and the merge finishes early with a badly truncated, wrong result — with no error raised
mcqs.explanation: The invariant this algorithm depends on is that the heap always holds one candidate per still-active source; skipping the re-push breaks that invariant for the affected source, which then contributes nothing further — the merge terminates as soon as the heap empties, well before all elements are actually output, with no exception thrown. Heaps have no self-correcting mechanism for a missing push, and the bug has nothing to do with duplicate values between sources.

mcqs.question: Why does a heap-based k-way merge achieve O(n log k) instead of the O(nk) a naive linear-scan-per-step approach would cost?
options: The heap operation to find the current minimum costs O(log k) instead of a linear O(k) scan across all sources, and this happens once per output element across n total elements
The heap-based approach processes fewer than n total elements
O(nk) and O(n log k) are actually the same complexity written differently
The heap-based approach only works when k equals n
mcqs.explanation: Both approaches examine every output element, so the difference is purely in how the minimum is found at each step — an O(k) linear scan versus an O(log k) heap operation — and multiplying that per-step cost by n total elements gives the respective O(nk) versus O(n log k) totals. These are genuinely different complexity classes (log k grows far slower than k), and the heap-based approach works for any relationship between n and k.

mcqs.question: Heap-based k-way merge and pairwise tournament-round merging both achieve O(n log k). What's the actual basis for choosing between them?
options: There's no real difference — one is always strictly faster than the other
Constant-factor and implementation trade-offs — the heap version is often simpler to write in one pass, while pairwise merging can be more memory-efficient for linked-list sources merged in place
Pairwise merging only works for exactly 2 lists, never more
The heap-based approach cannot be used with linked lists, only arrays
mcqs.explanation: Since both hit the same asymptotic bound, the choice comes down to constants and implementation convenience rather than correctness — the heap version tends to be a simpler single loop, while pairwise merging avoids heap bookkeeping overhead and can merge linked lists in place more efficiently. Pairwise merging generalizes to any number of lists via tournament rounds, and the heap-based approach works fine with linked-list sources too, just with different bookkeeping.

mcqs.question: You're merging 500 sorted lists of 4 elements each with a size-K heap. Why might a plain linear scan across the current fronts actually beat the heap here?
options: Linear scans are always asymptotically faster than heap operations regardless of K
The heap-based algorithm is only correct when all lists have equal length
When K is large relative to the total input, a linear scan's O(K) per step can lose to O(log K) at any scale
With K this large relative to the total data, the heap's per-operation bookkeeping overhead can outweigh the O(log K) vs O(K) asymptotic gap in practice
mcqs.explanation: The O(log k) vs O(k) comparison is about asymptotic growth, but at small absolute scale the heap's constant-factor overhead (tuple comparisons, swaps, index bookkeeping) can outweigh a simple, cache-friendly linear scan across a modest number of fronts. Equal list lengths aren't required for correctness, and a linear scan doesn't magically become asymptotically faster — this is purely a constant-factor, small-K argument.
